Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: THE DISPOSITIONAL BASIS OF SERVANT LEADERSHIP

text.text: Bart Wille obtained his PhD from Ghent University in 2013.
His research focuses on individual differences in the work context.
Specific topics include the role of personality in career choice, job attitudes, work performance, and leader effectiveness.

The concept of leaders acting as servants was first introduced by Greenleaf (1977) and has since attracted considerable scholarly attention (e.g., Lee, Lyubovnikova, et al., 2020; Lemoine et al., 2019).

text.text: Servant leadership is commonly defined as "an other-oriented approach to leadership manifested through one-on-one prioritizing of follower individual needs and interests and outward reorienting of their concern for self towards concern for others within the organization and the larger community" (Eva et al., 2019, p. 114).

text.text: Research has linked servant leadership to a range of positive outcomes at the individual, team, and organizational levels (e.g., Eva et al., 2019; Hoch et al., 2018).

Participants were Belgian subordinates and supervisors working across diverse sectors and organizations.
Dyads were recruited through the personal networks of bachelor's and master's psychology students.
To be eligible, participants had to (a) work at least 4/5 time, (b) be at least 21 years old, (c) have at least two years of work experience, and (d) occupy either a subordinate or supervisor role.
Two recruitment procedures were used.
In the first procedure, subordinates received an information letter inviting them to participate in a study on motivation and leadership.
The letter included a brief study description, information about the survey, a personal code to link dyadic responses, and a link to the online survey.
Approximately one week later, researchers invited supervisors by email after subordinates had provided their contact information.
To protect privacy, subordinates were required to obtain their supervisors' consent before sharing their email addresses.
The second procedure followed the same logic but started with supervisors.
Supervisors were asked to provide the email address of the subordinate with whom they had worked the longest.
Researchers then invited these subordinates after collecting their contact information through the supervisor survey.
The research project received ethics approval from XXX (blinded for peer review) ethical committee (2020/163).
The supervisor survey consisted of two modules: (a) a traditional survey with demographic questions and explicit measures and (b) the implicit measures.
Given the intensity of the design, supervisors could complete both modules separately within a two-week period.
We employed varying incentives during the data collection process.
Depending on the recruitment wave, participants received either the chance to win a gift voucher or immediate personalized feedback as compensation.
A total of 273 subordinates and 260 supervisors completed the questionnaires.
After excluding participants who did not meet the inclusion criteria, 229 dyads remained.
To ensure data quality, we further excluded participants who failed the control items that were placed at various points in the surveys (e.g., "Please respond with "Disagree" for this item").
The final sample included 219 complete dyads.
Subordinates (62.1% female) were between 21 and 64 years old (M = 42.36, SD = 11.40) and had worked in their organization for an average of 12.93 years (SD = 10.38).
Most were highly educated, with 73.5% holding a bachelor's or master's degree.
Supervisors (50.2% female) were between 21 and 66 years old (M = 46.12, SD = 9.96) and reported an average organizational tenure of 16.43 years (SD = 10.94).
Similar to subordinates, most supervisors were highly educated (86.8% held a bachelor's or master's degree).

The average dyadic tenure between subordinates and their supervisor was 6.15 years (SD = 6.18), and approximately half of the subordinates (49.3%) reported being in contact daily with their supervisor.

Finally, participants in this study worked in diverse industries such as trades and services (21.9%), engineering, production, and construction (21.5%), healthcare and well-being (16.0%), education, culture, and science (15.1%), and law, security, and public administration (14.1%).

Therefore, Hypothesis 2 could not be supported.
Hypotheses 3a-c predicted that power and affiliation motives would be positively related to servant leadership, whereas the achievement motive would be negatively related.

The primary objective of this study was to advance the servant leadership literature by examining leaders' explicit traits, implicit motives, and their interplay as antecedents of servant leadership.

Specifically, we assessed leaders' self-rated explicit personality traits using the HEXACO personality framework (Ashton & Lee, 2009), which enabled us to include Honesty-Humility alongside traits that have previously been linked to servant leadership (e.g., Hunter et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Specifically, we assessed leaders' self-rated explicit personality traits using the HEXACO personality framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Ashton & Lee, 2009)</ref>, which enabled us to include Honesty-Humility alongside traits that have previously been linked to servant leadership (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Hunter et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, we investigated whether leaders' implicit motives (i.e., the power, affiliation, and achievement motive) explained variance in servant leadership beyond these explicit traits.

Drawing on the channeling hypothesis (Lang et al., 2012; Winter et al., 1998), we further examined whether explicit traits interact with (corresponding) implicit motives and whether these interactions improve the prediction of servant leadership.
text.formatted: Drawing on the channeling hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Lang et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Winter et al., 1998)</ref>, we further examined whether explicit traits interact with (corresponding) implicit motives and whether these interactions improve the prediction of servant leadership.

text.text: Contrary to our expectations, neither the HEXACO personality traits nor the implicit motives emerged as significant predictors of servant leadership.
However, incorporating the channeling effects significantly increased the explained variance in servant leadership.

Consistent with our hypothesis, we found support for a channeling effect of extraversion on the relationship between leaders' affiliation motive and servant leadership, such that affiliationoriented leaders displayed higher levels of servant leadership only when they were also highly extraverted.
In contrast, no support was found for the hypothesized channeling effect of extraversion on implicit power.
Finally, agreeableness significantly moderated the relationship between implicit affiliation and servant leadership, although not in the hypothesized direction.
Specifically, affiliation-oriented leaders exhibited higher levels of servant leadership when they were lower rather than higher in agreeableness.

One possible explanation is that leaders who are relatively low in agreeableness, yet strongly motivated to develop and maintain close interpersonal relationships, may be more willing to address problems, confront difficult issues, and provide candid feedback when necessary.
Although such behaviors may sometimes be perceived as less accommodating, they may ultimately promote followers' growth and development.
In this regard, Heine et al. (2018) described a combination of support and challenge as "tough love" within the servant leadership context.
text.formatted: In this regard, <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Heine et al. (2018)</ref> described a combination of support and challenge as "tough love" within the servant leadership context.

text.text: Alternatively, servant behaviors displayed by these leaders may be perceived as more genuine, thereby strengthening followers' perceptions of servant leadership.
The non-significant relationships between explicit traits and servant leadership in the present study add nuance to prior research on these associations.
Overall, research on the relationship between servant leadership and personality traits using dyadic designs is relatively limited.

Specifically, studies using similar designs have shown that leaders' agreeableness is positively associated with followers' perceptions of servant leadership (Sun & Shang, 2019; Washington et al., 2006), whereas leaders' extraversion is negatively associated with such perceptions (Hunter et al., 2013).

text.text: One potential explanation for the non-significant relationship between agreeableness and servant leadership concerns differences in measurement.

Whereas prior studies relied on Big Five conceptualizations of agreeableness, we used HEXACO Agreeableness, which differs conceptually by excluding sentimentality-related content and incorporating anger-related tendencies typically captured by Neuroticism in the Big Five framework (Ashton et al., 2014).

text.text: The non-significant relationships between implicit motives and servant leadership are also noteworthy.

Although we are not aware of prior research directly examining these associations, significant links have been found between the affiliation motive and related leadership constructs such as transformational leadership (Steinmann et al., 2015 (Steinmann et al., , 2020)).

text.text: Contrary to these expectations, implicit motives did not exhibit direct relationships with servant leadership in the present study.

However, the significant interaction effects suggest that affiliation motives may not influence servant leadership in isolation but rather in combination with corresponding explicit personality traits (i.e., agreeableness and extraversion).

The emergence of these effects across raters is particularly noteworthy because it reduces concerns that the findings are driven by common method bias (Podsakoff et al., 2024) and suggests that the proposed channeling mechanisms are reflected in how leaders are actually perceived by their followers.

text.text: Taken together, these findings advance understanding of how implicit and explicit personality jointly influence servant leadership. Hunter and colleagues (2013, p. 327) proposed that the different impact of agreeableness and extraversion on servant leadership may stem from "underlying motivations and values (communion striving and status striving) that drive servant leader behavior" and called for future research to examine this possibility.

text.text: Our findings suggest that leaders were perceived as more servant-oriented only when their extraverted behavior aligned with a strong implicit need for affiliation.

This channeling effect is consistent with prior research in other domains (e.g., Lang et al., 2012; Winter et al., 1998) and may help explain the previously observed negative association between extraversion and servant leadership (Hunter et al., 2013).

text.text: As Lang et al. (2012) argued, extraverted behavior may facilitate the initiation of relationships, but without a strong affiliation motive it may be insufficient to sustain them over time.

text.text: Our findings may also help explain inconsistent results regarding the role of implicit affiliation in positive leadership styles (House et al., 1991; McClelland, 1975; Steinmann et al., 2016 Steinmann et al., , 2020)).

text.text: Specifically, a strong need for affiliation was associated with higher servant leadership only when combined with high extraversion and low agreeableness.
This pattern suggests that affiliation motives may need to be complemented by more dominant and assertive attributes to translate into effective leadership.

Such an interpretation is consistent with research showing that the combination of communal (i.e., caring) and agentic (i.e., assertive, harsh) attributes can enhance leader effectiveness (e.g., Do & Minbashian, 2014; Micevski et al., 2017).

text.text: The current findings encourage organizations to consider both explicit personality traits and implicit motives in talent management practices.
Compared to explicit personality assessments, implicit motives have traditionally been underutilized because their assessment often requires substantial time and trained coders.
By eliminating the need for expert coders, the MSC (Runge & Lang, 2019) offers a practical and promising alternative.
text.formatted: By eliminating the need for expert coders, the MSC <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Runge & Lang, 2019)</ref> offers a practical and promising alternative.

text.text: First, organizations may benefit from incorporating both implicit and explicit personality assessments into leadership selection and promotion decisions.
Doing so could help identify individuals who possess not only the traits but also the underlying motivational drives associated with servant leadership.

Assessing both explicit and implicit traits may also support leadership training and development by providing leaders with insight into their strengths and development needs, thereby enabling more targeted interventions.

For example, introverted leaders who are strongly motivated to build and maintain close relationships may benefit from training aimed at enhancing social and assertive behaviors (e.g., Haehner et al., 2024).
text.formatted: For example, introverted leaders who are strongly motivated to build and maintain close relationships may benefit from training aimed at enhancing social and assertive behaviors (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Haehner et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Likewise, highly affiliation-motivated leaders who score very high on agreeableness may benefit from conflict management training to offset potential drawbacks associated with excessive agreeableness.

Finally, because servant leadership is linked to a range of positive individual, team, and organizational outcomes (Eva et al., 2019; Hoch et al., 2018; Lee, Lyubovnikova, et al., 2020), a better understanding of its antecedents may ultimately help organizations foster more effective leadership and become more competitive.

text.text: The present study possesses several notable strengths.

First, it contributes to a relatively underdeveloped area of research by examining leaders' implicit motives, which are rarely included in leadership studies due to the resource-intensive nature of their assessment.
Given the substantial time commitment required from participants (approximately 60 minutes in the present study), obtaining a relatively large sample of supervisors represents a significant strength.
Second, the study employed a multi-informant leader-follower design, with leaders reporting their own personality characteristics and followers rating servant leadership.
This design reduces concerns regarding common method bias (Podsakoff et al., 2024) and provides a particularly rigorous test of the proposed relationships.
text.formatted: This design reduces concerns regarding common method bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Podsakoff et al., 2024)</ref> and provides a particularly rigorous test of the proposed relationships.

text.text: Finally, participants were drawn from a wide range of organizations and occupational backgrounds, increasing confidence that the observed relationships generalize across different organizational contexts.
Despite these strengths, several limitations should be considered.
First, the crosssectional design prevents causal inference.
Recent reviews have emphasized the value of research designs that allow for stronger causal conclusions in servant leadership research (Schowalter & Volmer, 2023).
text.formatted: Recent reviews have emphasized the value of research designs that allow for stronger causal conclusions in servant leadership research <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Schowalter & Volmer, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Although implicit motives and personality traits tend to be relatively stable, the possibility that servant leadership itself contributes to personality development over time cannot be excluded.
Additionally, our design provides only a snapshot of leaders' implicit and explicit personality characteristics and perceived leadership style at a single point in time.
As a result, it remains unclear how and when followers infer and use information about their leaders' underlying motives.
Second, it is important to note that the overall amount of variance explained in servant leadership was relatively modest.
This finding is consistent with prior leadership research, in which personality traits generally show only modest associations with leadership styles (e.g., Bono & Judge, 2004).
text.formatted: This finding is consistent with prior leadership research, in which personality traits generally show only modest associations with leadership styles (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bono & Judge, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: As noted by De Vries (2012), such effects may be attenuated by the limited correspondence between self-rated personality and other-rated leadership.

At the same time, the modest explained variance indicates that servant leadership is likely influenced by a broader constellation of individual and contextual factors than those included in the present study.
Drawing on these limitations, we believe this study presents potential opportunities for future research.
First, prospective studies could examine other potentially relevant variables (e.g., contextual variables, follower attributes) to improve the prediction of servant leadership.
In particular, more attention should be devoted to factors that moderate the relationship between leader characteristics and servant leadership.

For instance, followers' expectations toward their leaders (e.g., ideal leader prototype; Lacroix & Verdorfer, 2017) and sensitivity to favorable treatment (Wu et al., 2013) may provide valuable insights into earlier stages of the leadership process.
text.formatted: For instance, followers' expectations toward their leaders (e.g., ideal leader prototype; <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Lacroix & Verdorfer, 2017)</ref> and sensitivity to favorable treatment <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Wu et al., 2013)</ref> may provide valuable insights into earlier stages of the leadership process.

text.text: Second, future research could extend our knowledge of implicit motives by examining their visibility to others.

While personality research routinely incorporates self-and otherratings of explicit traits (Connelly & Ones, 2010) little is known about whether implicit motives can be accurately perceived by followers.
text.formatted: While personality research routinely incorporates self-and otherratings of explicit traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Connelly & Ones, 2010)</ref> little is known about whether implicit motives can be accurately perceived by followers.

text.text: The leadership arena-reputation-identity (LARI) model (Vergauwe et al., 2022) offers a useful framework for investigating this issue.
text.formatted: The leadership arena-reputation-identity (LARI) model <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Vergauwe et al., 2022)</ref> offers a useful framework for investigating this issue.

text.text: Specifically, comparing leaders' self-rated implicit motives with followers' perceptions of these motives could help determine whether implicit motives are observable and the extent to which they shape leadership perceptions.
Finally, future research could employ longitudinal designs to examine how implicit motives and explicit traits jointly influence perceptions of servant leadership over time.
While explicit traits may be readily observable, implicit motives may only become visible through repeated interactions, allowing followers to revise or confirm their initial impressions of leaders.
For instance, low agreeableness may be perceived less negatively when followers start recognizing an underlying motivation to build and maintain meaningful relationships.
Such reevaluations may strengthen perceptions of servant leadership, particularly when leaders' behavior is perceived as sincere (Ma et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Such reevaluations may strengthen perceptions of servant leadership, particularly when leaders' behavior is perceived as sincere <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Ma et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Studying these temporal dynamics could enhance our understanding of how servant leadership perceptions emerge and unfold over time.
Despite the surge of interest in servant leadership over the past decades, its antecedents remain relatively underexplored.
Our research addresses this gap and highlights the benefits of considering the joint and interactive effects of implicit and explicit motives in the (servant) leadership field.

Overall, the findings suggest that a combination of specific traits-high implicit affiliation, high extraversion, and low agreeableness-can help gain a better understanding of what drives leaders to serve.
